$comment: THE SAME TEST, FOR ALL SIX LANGUAGES. Drift ships six SDKs so a customer can
build in the language their team already uses, and that promise is worth
exactly as much as the weakest one. Six independently-worded test suites can
each pass while asserting subtly different things — which is how Go came to
round-trip a local blob correctly while the other five silently did not.
So the assertions live HERE, once, and each language ships a thin driver that
performs the operations and prints what it got. check.py compares the two.
A language cannot quietly hold a weaker opinion about what correct means.
Every case runs against the LOCAL store — no BACKBONE_URL, no running slice —
because that is the loop a developer meets first and the one where the six
drifted apart. The edge cases call a loopback peer each driver stands up, which
echoes the path it was asked for and the X-Drift-Slice header it received.
The queue_ cases ALSO run against a real slice: `run.sh --slice <backbone url>`
hands each driver the slice's Backbone and checks the queue_ cases alone. The
slice is the authority on the queue wire, so the same expectations hold the
local store to what the slice answers.
The "$loop" section at the end is the one place that says what an SDK that
serves many calls from one process must do. check.py skips it; loop_check.py

declared_queue_pop_empty.why: A queue the Driftfile declares exists before anything runs: `drift file apply` creates it on a slice, and the CLI names it in DRIFT_DECLARED_QUEUES for a local run. The driver declares conformance-declared that way and pops it without pushing: it is empty, not missing. A Field polling its queue from its first tick otherwise works on a slice and fails on a laptop. Local only: on a slice, declaring is apply's job. queue_pop_never_pushed is the control.

queue_pop_never_pushed.why: A queue nothing was ever pushed to does not exist on a slice, which answers 404. A local store that called it empty let a consumer polling a misspelled queue wait forever on a laptop and fail only once deployed.

queue_error_carries_the_refusal.why: A refused call's error carries the status and the slice's own words. The driver pops a queue that does not exist and reports whether the error says `HTTP 404` and `not found`. Python's error dropped the slice's text, and Ruby's and PHP's dropped the status, so a caller could not tell a missing queue from any other failure without a debugger.

queue_push_ids.why: Push returns the id the slice gave the message, which a slice numbers from "0" per queue. Go, Python, PHP and Rust discarded it, and Node and Ruby returned the whole reply object, so no two SDKs handed the caller the same thing.

queue_len_never_pushed.why: The length of a queue that does not exist is the same 404, not a zero that reads as an idle queue.

queue_push_not_an_object.why: A slice refuses a message body that is not a JSON object with a 400. A local store that accepted a bare string let code pass on a laptop that every slice refuses.

queue_push_bad_name.why: A queue name must start with a letter or digit, because it becomes a directory on the slice. `-flag` is refused there, so it is refused locally.

queue_len_after_push.why: Three pushes make three waiting messages.

queue_peek.why: Peek reads the head without removing it. Before this, no SDK had a Peek, although the slice has always served one.

queue_len_after_peek.why: THE CONTROL for peek: a peek that removed the message would read as a correct peek above and show up here as 2.

queue_pop_in_order.why: Pop returns the body each message was pushed with, first in first out. Every SDK named the queue in a pop's JSON body, which the slice never reads, so on a slice every pop was refused with 400 'queue query param required' and only the local store ever answered.

queue_pop_empty.why: An empty queue answers 204, which every SDK returns as its own empty value rather than an error: callers branch on 'nothing was waiting'.

queue_peek_empty.why: The same empty answer for a peek.

queue_len_after_pop.why: The queue is empty and still exists, so its length is 0 rather than the 404 of a queue that never did.

blob_with_bucket.why: Put then Get must return the bytes. The failure shape being guarded against is a Put that reports success and a Get that returns empty with no error — indistinguishable from 'I stored an empty value'.

blob_without_bucket.why: A bare name has no bucket, so it lands in the default one and must come back from there rather than from whatever the slash-splitting produced.

blob_absent.why: THE CONTROL, and the sharpest case here. A key that was never written must FAIL — Go answers a 404 — and the driver reports the string "error" when the call raises. An SDK that returns empty-with-no-error instead reports null and fails this case, which is exactly the defect the two cases above cannot catch on their own: an implementation that returns empty for EVERYTHING passes both of them by accident.

list_in_order.why: ListInOrder exists solely to fix the order a plain List returns. Twelve documents, inserted 1..12, must come back 1..12.

list_default_order.why: THE CONTROL for the one above, and the contract a paging caller already holds. The DEFAULT read is byte order over the storage key, which for twelve documents is 1,10,11,12,2,…,9 — documented behaviour, not a bug. Adding the ordered variant must not change it.

list_all_in_order_count.why: ListAllInOrder pages, so the ordered cursor has to advance in the ordered sequence rather than in key order. 1200 documents crosses the 1000-row page cap, which is where a cursor that advances by key silently truncates.

list_all_in_order_first.why: The first document of the first page.

list_all_in_order_boundary.why: The document either side of the page boundary is where a wrong cursor loses or repeats rows.

list_all_in_order_last.why: The last document of the last page.

list_filter_two_fields.why: A filter with two entries returns the documents matching BOTH, as a slice does. Of x1 (a=1,b=1), x2 (a=1,b=2), x3 (a=2,b=1) and x4 (a=3,b=2), only x2 has a=1 AND b=2. An SDK honouring one entry answers two documents — the first entry's pair or the last's — and a handler acting on that touches records it never asked for.

list_filter_one_field.why: THE CONTROL for the one above. A single entry reads exactly as it always has: a=1 is x1 and x2. Without it, an SDK that returned x2 for every filter would pass the case above.

list_filter_over_cap.why: A slice refuses a filter of more than 8 entries with a 400, so a local run refuses it too. The document matches all nine entries, so an SDK that applies no cap answers it rather than failing. Rust's list has no error channel and reads any refusal as no rows, the same way it reads a slice's 400; its driver reports that as the error.

edge_slice_url.why: Edge.Slice(name) reaches the slice a link names. The driver links `billing-api` by setting DRIFT_LINK_BILLING_API_URL to a loopback peer under /base/, calls GET /api/events, and reports the path the peer saw. The name's dash becomes an underscore in the variable, and the base path is kept, so a wrong variable or a dropped base both show here.

slice_url.why: THE CONTROL for the one above, and the alias contract: the deprecated Slice(name) spelling must keep working and reach the same link. An SDK whose Edge spelling read a different variable would pass one of these two and fail the other.

edge_slice_not_linked.why: A slice with no link refuses before any network I/O, and the refusal names where a link is declared: edge.links in the Driftfile, the only place one is declared. The text is the same in all six languages so a developer reads one message whichever SDK they use.
edge_slice_not_linked.expect: drift: slice "billing" is not linked: declare it under edge.links in the Driftfile

slice_not_linked.why: The deprecated spelling refuses with the same message, because it is the same client.
slice_not_linked.expect: drift: slice "billing" is not linked: declare it under edge.links in the Driftfile

slice_identity_absent.why: With no DRIFT_SLICE in the environment, which is the normal case for a function, the call carries NO X-Drift-Slice header. An empty header asserts an identity of "" rather than none, and reads as a real answer to anything checking for presence. The peer reports null when the header is absent.

slice_identity_kept.why: With DRIFT_SLICE=billing, a caller passing its own X-Drift-Slice: operator must not relabel the call. The header is a label and authorises nothing either way, but an SDK that lets the caller's copy win, or sends both, hands code a documented way to pose as another slice.

comment: THE LOOP A SLICE'S WARM WORKER SPEAKS, for every SDK that serves many calls
from one process. loop_check.py starts a small program per language (the
handler programs beside the drivers, each calling the SDK's own run entry)
with DRIFT_RUNTIME=1 and nothing else in its environment, sends it envelopes
over a pipe and compares what happens with `expect` below. check.py does not
read this section: its cases are the primitives, and these are a conversation.
The protocol is warmpool.rs and protocol.rs in cloud/platform: one JSON
envelope per line in, exactly one line out, the next envelope only after the
reply, end of input ends the process with status 0, and a trigger's one-shot
spawn sends one envelope with no trailing newline and closes stdin.
A case is a `session` (serve: calls, then end of input; one_shot; failure:
the last call's handler fails), the `calls` it sends, what to `observe` and
what to `expect`. A call may carry `tmpdir`, `secrets`, `secrets_previous`,
`print` (the handler writes that text to stdout) and `fail` (the handler
raises or panics); a member left out is left out of the envelope, as a slice
leaves out what it has nothing to say for. `only_on` limits a case to a
platform.
not_applicable: languages whose calls never reach the SDK's run entry. Not
run.
pending: languages whose loop is not built. The cases run and failing is
reported, not failed; passing FAILS until the language is taken off this
list, so the list cannot rot. Every other language must pass.

pending.rust: drift_sdk::run reads one envelope, answers it and returns: it does not loop yet.
pending.ruby: Drift.run reads one envelope, answers it and returns: it does not loop yet.

not_applicable.python: A deployed Python call reaches the slice's language server, which imports the function and calls its handler; the SDK's run entry is not on that path, so there is no loop of the SDK's own to hold to these cases.
not_applicable.node: A deployed Node call reaches the slice's language server, which imports the function and calls its handler; the SDK's run entry is not on that path, so there is no loop of the SDK's own to hold to these cases.

loop_one_reply_per_envelope.why: A warm worker serves many calls from one process: the slice writes an envelope, reads exactly one line back, then writes the next. A program that answers the first and exits, or answers it and swallows the rest, leaves the next call waiting until its runtime budget ends, and the slice cannot tell that from a slow function.

loop_one_process.why: The point of the loop is that the process stays: its sandbox and language runtime are paid for once. Five calls answered by five processes are five spawns behind one wrapper, and the slice would be keeping a worker that saves nothing. Each reply reports the pid of the process that served it, and it must be the one the controller started.

loop_tmpdir_and_home_are_the_envelopes.why: The slice makes a scratch directory for each call, removes it afterwards and names it in the envelope's tmpdir. A one-shot child gets it as TMPDIR and HOME at spawn; a warm worker was spawned once, so the SDK points both at each envelope's directory before the handler runs. One left on the first call's directory writes into a directory the slice has already removed, or one the next call shares.

loop_secret_is_what_the_envelope_carries.why: The slice sends the current value of every declared secret in every envelope, because a rotation can happen between two calls of one process. The SDK reads DRIFT_SECRET_<NAME> from the environment, so each envelope's values replace the last call's, and a secret that first appears in a later call is set in that call.

loop_secret_removed_when_not_carried.why: A secret deleted from the store stops being carried, and the next call must not be able to read it: a stale variable is indistinguishable from a live one to the accessor, so a process that only ever adds variables keeps serving a secret the tenant removed.

loop_previous_secret_follows_the_same_ru.why: Inside a rotation's grace window the envelope carries the replaced value as secrets_previous, and the SDK exposes it as DRIFT_SECRET_<NAME>_PREVIOUS. The envelope stops carrying it when the window ends, and the variable has to go in that call, or the worker keeps accepting a credential that was retired. The current value is carried throughout, so this case isolates the _PREVIOUS variable.

loop_a_printed_line_reaches_stderr_only.why: The response stream is the slice's: one reply line per call. A function that prints is logging, and the slice reads the process's stderr as the function's log. A printed line on the response stream is read as the reply, or desynchronises every call after it, and the slice retires a worker over a stray line. The first call prints; both calls must still be answered, and the text must be on stderr.

loop_reply_carries_rss_bytes.why: Nothing exits for the slice to weigh with wait4, so a warm worker reports its own peak resident size in every reply, and the slice's sizing and eviction read it. A worker that reports nothing makes its function's memory read as zero. Asserted on Linux, where a deployed function runs.

loop_eof_ends_the_process.why: Closing stdin is how the slice retires a worker. A process that ignores it stays until the slice kills it, and one that exits with a non-zero status makes a clean retirement look like a crash. After three answered calls and end of input the process must exit with status 0 within a second.

loop_one_shot_spawn.why: A trigger's or a cron's spawn runs the same program: it sends ONE envelope with no trailing newline and closes stdin at once. The program must answer that envelope, without waiting for a newline that never comes, and exit with status 0 when its input ends.

loop_a_failing_handler_ends_the_process.why: A handler that raises or panics ends the process, as it does in a one-shot spawn, and writes nothing more to the response stream. The slice sees the pipe close, reports how the process ended from its exit status and its stderr, and gives the next call a fresh worker. A process that survives is in a state nobody knows, one that answers for the failed call hides the failure, and a fatal error printed to stdout (PHP's display_errors) arrives as a stray line instead of the closed pipe the slice reports from.
